messages.content: I want to design a network diagnosis system that separates concurrent causal faults from downstream symptoms, even when routing is asymmetric and telemetry is incomplete.

The key distinction is between faults that could independently contribute to an incident and observations that may be consequences of those faults. The system should not treat every observed problem as another cause, but it also should not force multiple concurrent causes into a single-cause explanation. Asymmetric routing and missing telemetry make that distinction harder: an observation may reflect only one direction of traffic, and an unobserved condition is not necessarily absent.
What does it mean to separate concurrent faults from downstream symptoms without assuming there is always one root cause?

It means keeping causal candidates distinct from the effects they might explain. If more than one fault could be active at the same time, the diagnosis should be able to represent that possibility rather than selecting one fault merely because it accounts for a visible symptom. Conversely, several symptoms might follow from a fault without each symptom being classified as an independent cause. The aim is to make the causal explanation fit the observations without treating the number of observed symptoms as the number of faults.
And asymmetric routing means the two traffic directions cannot just be treated as the same path, right?

Right. Under asymmetric routing, evidence about one direction does not automatically establish what happened in the other direction. A diagnosis that depends on a path should respect the direction to which its evidence applies. Otherwise, it could incorrectly attribute a downstream symptom to a fault on a path that the relevant traffic did not take.
How should incomplete telemetry affect the strength of a conclusion?

It should limit what the system claims to know. A missing observation is different from an observation that a condition did not occur. With incomplete telemetry, multiple fault sets may remain consistent with what is visible. The system can still localize a fault when the available evidence supports doing so, but it should preserve uncertainty where the missing evidence prevents a distinction.
There is also a performance requirement: at least 90% fault-localization precision at at least 80% incident coverage with 30% telemetry loss. How do those thresholds fit together?

They are simultaneous targets for the system under the stated 30% telemetry-loss condition: fault-localization precision of ≥90% while incident coverage is ≥80%. High precision alone would not satisfy the goal if the system localized faults in too few incidents; broad coverage alone would not satisfy it if too many localizations were wrong. The requirement does not, by itself, specify how ambiguous reports are scored, so that would need to be made explicit when evaluating the targets.
So it should not maintain precision by refusing to address almost every difficult incident.

Exactly. The ≥80% incident-coverage requirement prevents that from being treated as sufficient. At the same time, coverage does not justify presenting an unsupported single cause as certain. The design has to handle uncertainty in a way that is compatible with both targets, rather than relying on either blanket abstention or overconfident localization.
What should the output say if two possible fault sets are observationally indistinguishable?

It should report the indistinguishable fault sets as such. That tells the reader the available observations do not separate those alternatives. It should not choose one set and present it as the sole cause unless there is evidence supporting that distinction. The indistinguishability is relative to the observations available for that incident; it is not a claim that the fault sets are identical in every possible circumstance.
Could one of those sets contain concurrent faults while another contains just one candidate fault?

Conceptually, yes. If both sets remain consistent with the available observations and the telemetry cannot distinguish them, the system should not conceal that difference by collapsing them into a single-cause statement. Reporting the alternatives preserves both the possibility of concurrent causes and the limits of the evidence. It does not assert that every fault in every alternative actually occurred.
I do not want downstream symptoms promoted to causes simply because they are the clearest observations.

That is an important constraint on the diagnosis. Visibility and causal status are different: a downstream symptom can be well observed while its upstream cause remains uncertain. The system should distinguish what was observed from what is inferred to have caused it, and should make clear when a proposed fault is only one explanation consistent with the observations.
Does missing telemetry automatically make every diagnosis ambiguous?

No. Incomplete telemetry can leave some distinctions unresolved, but it does not imply that every fault set is indistinguishable. The question is whether the evidence that remains supports a particular localization or leaves multiple explanations observationally equivalent. The system should neither assume certainty despite a consequential gap nor assume uncertainty where the available evidence actually makes a distinction.
I want to be precise about what the 30% figure says. It is telemetry loss, not permission to lower either target.

Yes. The stated goal is ≥90% fault-localization precision at ≥80% incident coverage with 30% telemetry loss. The loss condition is part of the setting in which both thresholds must be achieved; it does not replace either threshold. Nothing in that statement specifies a particular pattern of loss, so the design discussion should not silently assume one.
How would you express the core design principle in plain language?

Explain the observed incident using the causal fault sets the evidence can support, while keeping downstream effects separate from causes. Account for the possibility of concurrent faults and for direction-dependent routing. Where missing telemetry leaves fault sets observationally indistinguishable, report that ambiguity instead of inventing a unique cause.
That sounds cautious. Does it still count as fault localization if the report names more than one possible set?

It can be an informative diagnostic report because it narrows the explanation to the fault sets consistent with the observations. But the requirement does not specify whether such a report counts toward incident coverage or how it contributes to fault-localization precision. Those scoring rules should be stated explicitly before claiming that the ≥90% and ≥80% targets have been met. The reporting requirement itself is clear: indistinguishable sets must not be turned into an unsupported single-cause explanation.
So the system has to be accurate about both its conclusions and their limits.

Yes. It needs to identify supported causal faults rather than mistake downstream symptoms for faults, allow concurrent faults where warranted, and respect the limits imposed by asymmetric routing and incomplete telemetry. Its performance target remains ≥90% fault-localization precision at ≥80% incident coverage with 30% telemetry loss, while its reports must preserve observationally indistinguishable fault sets rather than assert a single cause the evidence cannot support.
What concrete design would put those ideas together?

I would propose a forward/reverse-path causal factor graph. It would represent causal fault candidates and their possible downstream symptoms in a way that respects traffic direction, perform joint inference over fault sets rather than assuming one fault, use likelihoods that account for missing telemetry, and report fault sets that the available observations cannot distinguish.
Why specify both forward and reverse paths in the graph?

Because the evidence associated with traffic in one direction need not describe the path in the other direction. A forward/reverse-path representation gives the diagnosis a way to reason about each direction without silently treating them as identical. It can then associate a symptom with the direction relevant to that observation, rather than using evidence from one path as though it automatically applied to both.
Is this two unrelated diagnoses, one per direction?

No. The proposal is a causal factor graph with forward- and reverse-path information, not a requirement to issue two isolated answers. The paths need to remain distinguishable, while joint inference considers the fault explanations consistent with the observations as a whole. Keeping direction explicit does not prevent the graph from expressing relationships that are actually supported; it prevents symmetry from being assumed without support.
Explain what the causal factor graph contributes here, without assuming we have already built one.

As a proposed representation, it organizes candidate faults, observable symptoms, and the relationships used to evaluate possible explanations. The causal part matters because a downstream observation should not automatically be treated as a separate initiating fault. The factor-graph part provides a way to combine evidence and constraints when several candidate faults and symptoms must be considered together. This describes the intended role of the graph, not an implemented model or a demonstrated result.
Where do symptom-propagation factors fit?

They express how a proposed fault could give rise to downstream symptoms. That lets the diagnosis evaluate an explanation in which several observations are consequences of a fault, instead of counting every observation as a distinct cause. They also help test whether a proposed fault set coherently explains what is observed. Such factors encode hypothesized relationships for inference; their presence alone would not prove that a particular fault occurred.
Would propagation factors mean that every symptom has to be traced to one known fault?

No. The proposal should not force an unsupported attribution. Propagation factors help assess candidate explanations, but incomplete telemetry can leave the origin of a symptom unresolved, and concurrent faults can contribute to an incident. The graph should support uncertainty about which fault set caused an observation rather than manufacture a uniquely identified cause for every symptom.
Why joint fault inference instead of evaluating each candidate fault separately?

Independent, one-at-a-time evaluations can miss the possibility that multiple faults are present concurrently. Joint inference considers fault sets, so it can ask whether the observations fit a combination of faults and their downstream effects. It also helps avoid treating evidence explained by one candidate as though it necessarily excludes another. Joint inference is a design choice here; it does not mean every incident must have multiple causes.
Could joint inference also help avoid mistaking two symptoms for two faults?

That is part of the intent. A joint explanation can consider whether two observed problems are downstream effects of a candidate fault, whether they are associated with different concurrent faults, or whether the evidence cannot distinguish those possibilities. Symptom-propagation factors express the proposed causal relationships; joint inference evaluates combinations without making the number of symptoms dictate the number of causes.
What does 'missingness-aware likelihoods' commit us to?

It commits the proposed inference to distinguishing telemetry that is absent from telemetry that was present and showed no relevant condition. Missing observations should not be used as if they were negative evidence by default. The likelihoods should account for what was and was not observed when comparing fault explanations. The proposal does not specify a particular missing-data mechanism, likelihood formula, or source of telemetry loss.
Suppose a symptom is not visible. Can the graph conclude it did not happen?

Not merely because it is not visible. If the relevant telemetry is missing, the symptom's absence from the record does not establish its absence from the incident. A missingness-aware likelihood is meant to preserve that distinction. What the system can infer depends on the available observations and the likelihood relationships being modeled; it should not turn a monitoring gap into a factual claim.
How do these likelihoods interact with the forward and reverse paths?

They should evaluate evidence in light of both its direction and its availability. An observation concerning one path should not automatically count as an observation about the opposite path, and a missing observation on either path should not be treated as a confirmed negative. In the proposed graph, path-specific causal relationships and missingness-aware evidence assessment work together to limit claims to what the telemetry supports.
I also need the system to report indistinguishable fault sets. Is that separate from the inference?

It is an output requirement tied closely to inference. Joint inference may leave more than one fault set consistent with the available observations. If the evidence does not distinguish those sets, the report should preserve them as alternatives rather than select one and present it as the sole cause. The graph provides a proposed way to reason about candidates; indistinguishable-fault-set reporting makes the resulting uncertainty visible.
Does 'indistinguishable' mean the candidate fault sets must be exactly the same in the model?

No. They can be different fault sets whose relevant consequences cannot be told apart using the observations available for the incident. The qualification is observational: it describes a limit of the evidence, not an assertion that the underlying faults are identical. The report should communicate that distinction without claiming a unique explanation that the evidence does not support.
If one candidate explanation has one fault and another has concurrent faults, should the report still show both if the observations cannot distinguish them?

Yes. Joint inference should allow both kinds of fault set to be considered, and indistinguishable-fault-set reporting should retain both when the available observations cannot resolve the difference. It would be misleading to choose the single-fault alternative merely because it is simpler, or to choose the concurrent-fault alternative merely because several symptoms were observed. Neither conclusion follows from indistinguishability alone.
Does this proposal already establish that the diagnosis will meet the performance targets we discussed?

No. It is a proposed design for addressing the diagnosis problem, not evidence that the targets have been achieved. Its components address distinct difficulties: path direction, concurrent faults, propagation of symptoms, missing telemetry, and unresolved alternatives. Whether the resulting system meets its performance requirements would require evaluation; the proposal itself makes no such claim.
Can you restate the proposal in one connected description, without implying that any results are in hand?

Build a causal factor graph that keeps forward and reverse paths distinct, uses symptom-propagation factors to relate candidate faults to downstream observations, and jointly infers possible fault sets. Make its likelihoods aware of missing telemetry so unobserved conditions are not mistaken for confirmed absences. When the available evidence cannot distinguish different fault sets, report those alternatives rather than asserting an unsupported single cause. That is the proposed architecture and reporting behavior, not an implemented or validated outcome.
Which forward/reverse-path evidence would distinguish simultaneous link faults from propagated symptoms under 30% probe loss?

The most useful evidence would distinguish a problem associated with each candidate link from effects that appear only downstream of one candidate. Forward- and reverse-path observations need to be considered separately: a symptom seen in one direction does not, by itself, establish a fault on the reverse path. For simultaneous link faults, the available observations would need to support each proposed fault, rather than merely show multiple symptoms that one fault could propagate. With 30% probe loss, the qualification is essential: if the probes needed to make that distinction are missing, the system should report the remaining fault sets as indistinguishable.
What would count as evidence for each proposed link fault, rather than just another symptom?

Conceptually, it is evidence that differentiates explanations. An observation associated with traffic traversing a candidate link is more useful if observations on paths that do not traverse that link help separate its effect from a more general downstream effect. The question is whether the pattern supports a fault at that link independently of the symptoms attributed to another candidate fault. Merely observing problems at several downstream points would not establish several link faults.
So several affected observations are not enough on their own?

Correct. Several observations could be consequences of one fault, consequences of simultaneous faults, or consistent with both explanations. Their number does not decide their causal status. What matters is whether their forward/reverse-path relationships distinguish the competing fault sets: for example, whether an observation is associated with one candidate link but not explained just as a downstream consequence of the other. That is a question to evaluate against evidence, not a conclusion we can draw without it.
How does direction help make that distinction?

Direction helps prevent a misleading inference from a symptom on one path to a fault on another. If forward and reverse traffic take different paths, evidence from the forward direction can bear on a candidate forward-path link while saying little about a reverse-path link, and vice versa. Keeping the directions distinct makes it possible to ask whether there is separate support for faults on both paths or whether one observed symptom is being projected onto the other direction without evidence.
Does seeing symptoms in both directions prove there are simultaneous link faults?

No. Symptoms in both directions are observations to explain, not proof of two causal faults. Whether they support simultaneous link faults depends on which paths the observations concern, how a candidate fault could propagate symptoms, and whether another fault set explains the same evidence. If both a simultaneous-fault explanation and a propagated-symptom explanation remain observationally indistinguishable, the report should retain both.
What role do the symptom-propagation factors play in answering the evidence question?

They let the proposed factor graph ask whether a candidate fault could account for observations downstream without classifying those observations as additional faults. The graph can compare that explanation with one containing simultaneous link faults. Evidence distinguishes the two only if it favors one explanation in a way the other cannot equally account for under the available observations. The propagation factors describe relationships to assess; they do not turn an observed symptom into a proven cause.
And joint fault inference is what permits the simultaneous-fault explanation to be considered at all?

Yes. Joint inference can consider a fault set containing more than one link fault alongside other candidate sets. The distinction then depends on evidence, rather than an assumption that there must be exactly one cause. It should also avoid the opposite assumption: that different observed symptoms necessarily require different link faults.
How should 30% probe loss change the comparison?

It means the comparison must be made using the probes that remain, while accounting for probes that were lost. A lost probe is not an observation that its path was unaffected. If the missing probes would have supplied the directional or path-specific contrast needed to tell the explanations apart, the system cannot claim that contrast was observed. The 30% figure states how much probe loss is at issue; it does not specify which probes are lost or whether the loss is distributed in a particular way.
Could the remaining 70% be enough?

Possibly, but the percentage alone cannot answer that. What matters for this question is whether the remaining observations include the forward/reverse-path evidence that differentiates the candidate fault sets. Losing probes that carry the decisive contrast can leave ambiguity even if many other probes remain; retaining that contrast may still permit a distinction. Neither outcome is guaranteed just by saying there is 30% probe loss.
I want the system to avoid treating missing probes as healthy paths.

That is exactly the distinction missingness-aware likelihoods are meant to preserve. An observed probe result can contribute evidence about its path. A probe that was lost supplies no equivalent result, so it should not be counted as confirming that the path was healthy or that an expected symptom was absent. The inference should reflect that gap when comparing simultaneous-fault and propagation explanations.
Can it ever call a symptom propagated if the observation at the suspected causal link is missing?

It may still consider propagation as a possible explanation, but it should not present an unobserved link fault as established simply because its downstream symptoms would fit. The remaining evidence might distinguish that explanation from alternatives, or it might not. If a simultaneous-link-fault set fits equally well at the level the available observations can resolve, the report should preserve that ambiguity rather than assert a single causal chain.
What is the central comparison the factor graph needs to make?

It needs to compare whether the available forward- and reverse-path observations are better explained as effects propagated from a candidate fault or as evidence requiring simultaneous link faults. That comparison must account for which directional paths the observations actually describe and which probe results are missing. The decisive question is not simply how many symptoms appear, but whether the observed path relationships separate the candidate fault sets.
If they do not separate the sets, what should the diagnosis say?

It should identify the fault sets that remain observationally indistinguishable under the available probe evidence. It can explain that the missing or non-discriminating forward/reverse-path observations prevent a supported choice between simultaneous link faults and propagated symptoms. It should not turn one of those possibilities into a definite single-cause account.
Does observational indistinguishability mean the proposed faults are equally real?

No. It means the available observations do not resolve the difference between those candidate explanations. The underlying faults could differ, but the report should not claim to know which occurred when the evidence cannot tell. That distinction is particularly important under probe loss: uncertainty in what was observed is not itself evidence that any particular link fault did or did not happen.
Then the evidence I should ask for is directional and discriminating, not just more symptoms?

Yes. The useful question is whether the observed forward and reverse paths provide separate, path-relevant support for each candidate link fault, or instead show effects that a propagation explanation can also account for. Under 30% probe loss, ask that question only of results actually available, and preserve indistinguishable fault sets when those results cannot decide it.

Here is a hypothesis for the evidence question: forward/reverse path divergence and interface counters can distinguish concurrent faults from propagated symptoms at ≥90% fault-localization precision and ≥80% incident coverage under 30% loss.

That states a testable hypothesis, not an established result. Forward/reverse path divergence could help identify when observations in the two directions concern different paths. Interface counters could provide additional evidence associated with interfaces rather than relying only on downstream symptoms. The hypothesis is that, together, those forms of evidence distinguish concurrent faults from propagated symptoms while reaching both thresholds under the stated 30% loss condition.
What does forward/reverse path divergence add that the symptoms alone do not?

It makes a directional difference visible. If the forward and reverse paths diverge, a symptom associated with one direction cannot automatically be attributed to a link on the other. That can help separate evidence relevant to different candidate faults from symptoms that might propagate from one fault. Divergence alone does not establish that either candidate fault occurred; its value in the hypothesis is in making the competing explanations more distinguishable.
And why include interface counters?

They are a proposed second source of evidence to consider alongside path divergence. The idea is to examine whether counter observations associated with a candidate interface provide support that is not merely another downstream manifestation of a different fault. A counter reading would still need interpretation in its path and causal context; the mere presence of a counter observation would not prove a concurrent fault.
So the hypothesis is not that every difference between the two paths indicates two faults.

Correct. Forward/reverse path divergence describes a difference in the paths, not a count of faults. The proposed distinction depends on how that divergence and the interface-counter evidence bear on the competing explanations. The hypothesis would be overstated if it treated path divergence by itself as proof of concurrent faults.
How would those two evidence types help tell a concurrent fault from a propagated symptom?

Conceptually, they provide two questions to ask about a suspected second fault: does the relevant observation belong to a distinct forward or reverse path, and is there interface-counter evidence associated with the proposed fault rather than only symptoms that another fault could propagate? If the available evidence separates those explanations, it may support the distinction. If both fault sets still explain the observations, the evidence has not made the distinction, regardless of how many symptoms are visible.
I want the 30% loss condition kept in the claim, not treated as a minor caveat.

Yes. The hypothesis claims the ≥90% precision and ≥80% coverage thresholds under 30% loss, not merely when all evidence is present. Loss can remove observations needed to compare a concurrent-fault explanation with a propagated-symptom explanation. The hypothesis therefore depends on whether the evidence that remains is sufficiently discriminating; the 30% figure alone does not tell us which observations remain.
If an interface counter is unavailable because of that loss, should the diagnosis infer that nothing happened at the interface?

No. An unavailable counter is missing evidence, not a counter reading showing no relevant condition. Likewise, a lost probe is not a healthy-path observation. Missingness-aware inference should preserve those distinctions when assessing whether path divergence and the available counters actually distinguish the candidate fault sets.
Does this hypothesis claim that the two kinds of evidence will always identify a unique fault set?

No. It proposes that they can distinguish concurrent faults from propagated symptoms at the stated precision and coverage levels under 30% loss. It does not claim that every incident becomes uniquely identifiable. Where the available path and counter observations leave different fault sets observationally indistinguishable, the diagnosis should report those sets rather than assert a unique cause.
Could the precision target be met just by making a confident choice in the covered incidents?

Confidence alone would not establish ≥90% fault-localization precision. The precision target concerns the correctness of localizations, while ≥80% incident coverage requires the system to address a sufficiently large share of incidents under the same 30% loss condition. The hypothesis says both thresholds can be achieved; it does not provide results showing that they have been.
I also do not want an ambiguous report silently counted as a correct single-fault localization.

That is consistent with reporting indistinguishable fault sets honestly. An ambiguous report should not be described as a uniquely correct single-fault conclusion. How such reports contribute to precision and coverage would have to be defined for an evaluation; this hypothesis does not supply that scoring rule or an evaluation outcome.
Is the claim specifically about simultaneous link faults, or is 'concurrent faults' broader here?

The hypothesis says 'concurrent faults' and contrasts them with propagated symptoms. The motivating evidence question concerns simultaneous link faults, but the hypothesis does not specify a broader inventory of fault types. It is safest to keep the stated claim at that level: use forward/reverse path divergence and interface counters to distinguish concurrent causal faults from downstream effects, without adding unmentioned fault categories.
What if the paths diverge but the available counter evidence does not separate the explanations?

Then divergence has identified a relevant path distinction, but the available evidence may still be insufficient to decide whether there are concurrent faults or a propagated symptom. The hypothesis should not be converted into a rule that always picks one explanation whenever paths diverge. If the candidate fault sets remain observationally indistinguishable, the report should say so.
Can you phrase the hypothesis compactly while retaining every condition?

Hypothesis: forward/reverse path divergence together with interface counters distinguishes concurrent faults from propagated symptoms, achieving ≥90% fault-localization precision at ≥80% incident coverage under 30% loss. This remains a hypothesis to assess, and any fault sets that the available observations cannot distinguish should still be reported as indistinguishable.
How should we evaluate whether directional evidence separates concurrent faults from propagated symptoms?

Replay AsymFault-30 dual-fault and symptom-only incidents with directional probes, interface counters, and 30% dropout. Then measure localization precision and incident coverage. The replay is an evaluation activity: it would show how the diagnosis behaves under those conditions, not establish a result in advance.
Why include both dual-fault and symptom-only incidents?

They put the distinction at issue on both sides. In dual-fault incidents, the diagnosis needs to recognize concurrent faults rather than compress them into an unsupported single cause. In symptom-only incidents, it needs to avoid promoting downstream symptoms into additional faults. Replaying both lets the evaluation examine that distinction instead of assessing localization without regard to whether a second apparent problem is causal.
What is the role of the directional probes in the replay?

They supply observations whose forward or reverse direction matters. The evaluation can then examine whether the diagnosis uses evidence from the appropriate direction rather than assuming the paths are interchangeable. Their presence in the replay does not guarantee that every incident has enough directional evidence to distinguish its possible fault sets, especially with 30% dropout.
And the interface counters?

They provide another kind of observation to use alongside the directional probes when assessing candidate faults and downstream effects. The replay can test whether using those observations helps the diagnosis make supported distinctions. A counter observation still has to be interpreted in context; including counters does not make every apparent symptom evidence of a separate fault.
I want the dropout represented in the evaluation itself, not just mentioned afterward.

Agreed. The activity is to replay the AsymFault-30 incidents with 30% dropout while using the available directional probes and interface counters. Precision and coverage should be measured for diagnosis under that dropout condition. The activity does not specify which individual observations drop out or a particular dropout mechanism, so those details should not be assumed from the 30% figure alone.
Does 30% dropout mean the missing probe results should count as normal results?

No. Dropout removes observations; it does not turn them into evidence that a path was unaffected. During the replay, a distinction that depends on a missing observation cannot be treated as though it was observed. That matters when judging whether the diagnosis localized faults or merely chose among explanations the available evidence could not separate.
What exactly would localization precision tell us here?

It would assess the correctness of the fault localizations the diagnosis makes in the replay. For this activity, the important question is whether a reported causal fault is actually a fault in the replayed incident, rather than a downstream symptom incorrectly promoted to one. The node calls for measuring precision but does not specify the complete scoring rule, so we should not assume how every form of report is scored.
What would incident coverage add to that measurement?

Coverage would show how broadly the diagnosis provides a report counted as covering an incident, rather than measuring correctness only among a narrow set of localizations. Measuring both matters because a diagnosis could avoid difficult cases or, conversely, report widely without being precise. The evaluation activity calls for both metrics but does not itself define what qualifies a report for coverage.
Could the replay report precision and coverage separately for the two incident types?

That could help explain where a measured outcome comes from, but it is an optional way to examine the results, not an additional result or requirement stated for this activity. The specified activity is to replay AsymFault-30 dual-fault and symptom-only incidents under the stated evidence and dropout conditions, then measure localization precision and coverage. Any finer breakdown would need to remain consistent with those measurements.
What failure would we look for in a symptom-only incident?

The relevant failure would be localizing an additional causal fault solely because a propagated symptom was observed. The replay provides symptom-only incidents so that this error can be examined. We should not assume the diagnosis does or does not make that error before measuring its behavior.
And what would the dual-fault incidents reveal?

They would let the evaluation examine whether the diagnosis accounts for two concurrent faults when the replayed incident contains them, rather than attributing everything to one fault and treating the other as a symptom. Under 30% dropout, they also raise the question of whether the remaining directional-probe and counter observations support both localizations. The replay is how that behavior would be assessed, not evidence yet that it succeeds.
What if the observations remaining after dropout cannot distinguish a dual-fault explanation from a symptom-only one?

Then the diagnosis should not claim the observations uniquely establish one explanation. It should preserve the indistinguishable fault sets in its report. The evaluation would still need an explicit scoring rule for how that kind of report contributes to localization precision and incident coverage; the replay activity alone does not settle the scoring rule.
So reporting uncertainty and measuring performance are related but not identical tasks?

Exactly. The diagnosis should express what the available observations support, including ambiguity when appropriate. The replay measures its localization precision and coverage under 30% dropout. To interpret those measurements, the treatment of ambiguous reports has to be clear; otherwise a cautious report could be mistaken for a confident single-fault localization, or excluded without explanation.
Does the name AsymFault-30 tell us anything else about the dataset or its size?

Not from this activity statement. AsymFault-30 is the named source of the dual-fault and symptom-only incidents to replay. The specified evidence is directional probes and interface counters, with 30% dropout. No incident count, collection procedure, or other dataset properties are given here.
Please keep the evaluation description to what we actually plan to do, without implying any outcome.

Replay AsymFault-30 dual-fault and symptom-only incidents using directional probes and interface counters under 30% dropout, and measure localization precision and incident coverage. That activity evaluates whether the proposed diagnosis distinguishes concurrent faults from propagated symptoms under the stated conditions; it does not yet say what either metric will be.
What did the AsymFault-30 measurement show at 30% dropout?

On AsymFault-30 at 30% dropout, directional probes plus interface counters achieved 92% fault-localization precision and 83% incident coverage. Those are the measured values for that setting; the result does not give a breakdown by incident type.
Can you keep precision and coverage distinct when describing that result?

Yes. The reported fault-localization precision was 92%, and the reported incident coverage was 83%. Precision describes the localization measurement, while coverage describes how much of the incident set the measurement encompassed. They are two separate figures, both reported under 30% dropout.
Were those figures obtained with just directional probes?
No. The stated result is for directional probes plus interface counters. It does not report a probes-only result, so we cannot attribute the 92% precision or 83% coverage to directional probes alone.
Does the evidence isolate how much the interface counters contributed?

No. It reports the combined condition—directional probes plus interface counters—without a separate measurement of either evidence source. The result therefore does not quantify the individual contribution of the counters or the probes.
And the 30% figure refers to dropout in this result?

Correct. The reported 92% fault-localization precision and 83% incident coverage are specifically for AsymFault-30 at 30% dropout. The statement does not describe the dropout pattern or identify which observations were lost.
Can we tell from these aggregate numbers exactly which concurrent faults were distinguished from propagated symptoms?

No. The two aggregate measurements do not identify particular incidents, fault sets, or symptom relationships. They tell us the reported precision and coverage for the combined evidence in the stated setting, but not how any individual diagnosis was resolved.
Do the figures say how indistinguishable fault sets were handled?

Not on their own. This evidence statement gives the measured precision and coverage, but it does not specify the reporting format or scoring treatment for observationally indistinguishable fault sets. We should not infer from the aggregate numbers that every covered incident received a unique single-cause explanation.
Give me a concise statement of the result without adding claims about other settings.
On AsymFault-30 at 30% dropout, directional probes plus interface counters achieved 92% fault-localization precision and 83% incident coverage.
Given the AsymFault-30 result, what should we adopt for joint fault inference?

Adopt directional probes and interface counters for joint fault inference. The reason for that decision is that, on AsymFault-30 at 30% dropout, their combined use achieved 92% fault-localization precision and 83% incident coverage—exceeding both the ≥90% precision target and the ≥80% coverage target.
Why does the decision name both evidence sources?

Because the reported result is for directional probes plus interface counters together. It does not isolate a result for either source alone. The decision therefore adopts the combination for joint fault inference, without attributing the measured performance to just the probes or just the counters.
What does joint fault inference mean in this decision?

It means considering possible fault sets together, including the possibility of concurrent faults, rather than requiring every diagnosis to select exactly one fault. Directional probes and interface counters are the evidence sources being adopted for that inference. The decision does not say that every incident has multiple faults or that every candidate fault can be uniquely identified.
How do the measured numbers compare with the targets?

At 30% dropout on AsymFault-30, fault-localization precision was 92%, which is above the ≥90% target. Incident coverage was 83%, which is above the ≥80% target. Both comparisons apply to that reported setting and to the combined use of directional probes and interface counters.
Does 'despite 30% dropout' mean the decision assumes all telemetry was available?

No. The 30% dropout is part of the condition under which AsymFault-30 exceeded both targets. The decision rests on the result with that dropout, not on a result with complete telemetry. It does not specify which observations were lost or establish performance for every possible dropout pattern.
Are we claiming that the combination will exceed the targets in every network?

No. The stated basis for adoption is the AsymFault-30 result at 30% dropout. It supports the decision to use directional probes and interface counters for joint fault inference, but the decision does not supply measurements for other settings.
Does adopting them mean the system should always output one cause?

No. Joint fault inference allows the diagnosis to consider concurrent faults, and the reporting requirement remains to show observationally indistinguishable fault sets rather than assert an unsupported single cause. Adopting these evidence sources does not make ambiguity disappear in every incident.
